evidence.note: Built main.py in a deliberate section-by-section order that reflects a sensible dependency chain: constants/XML utils → storage helpers → SigV4 auth → audit/notification → policy eval → S3 routes → multipart/config handlers → admin API → lifecycle worker. Foundational auth/storage substrate was written before dependent features, and each 'Plan:' names the next discrete subsystem.

Verified basic signed CRUD (ListBuckets/CreateBucket/PutObject/GetObject) and then SigV4 rejection of bad credentials as an implicit gate before moving on to multipart/advanced features — an emergent 'done-check' per foundational milestone rather than a pre-declared acceptance criterion.

Testing proceeded in layered order — basic CRUD → multipart complete → versioning/tagging → presigned → admin API → console API → bucket configs → cross-tenant/quota — treating each subsystem as a discrete checkable unit, but the ordering was driven reactively by test results, not a stated milestone plan.

Closing checklist enumerates implemented subsystems with ✓ marks, showing the subsystem list was tracked; but this is a retrospective inventory, not an up-front milestone hierarchy with per-milestone acceptance criteria or the two grading surfaces scoped as separate tracks.

Long stretch of SigV4 query-string debugging where the same multi-item to-do ('fix dispatch, add locks, fix lifespan, fix payload hash…') is restated across many steps as a flat running list rather than a structured, risk-ordered milestone map — no explicit re-partitioning of the plan.

reasoning: The agent maintained a clear, reasonable dependency order — foundational SigV4 auth and storage substrate first, dependent features (multipart, versioning, configs, admin, console) layered after — and treated each subsystem as a discrete unit, matching the level-5 anchor. There is some emergent 'done-checking' (basic signed PUT/GET and auth rejection proven before multipart), nudging above a flat to-do list, but it falls short of level 8: milestones were never laid out as an explicit hierarchy with stated per-milestone acceptance checks, the two grading surfaces were not scoped as separate tracks, and the mid-trajectory planning devolved into a repeatedly-restated flat list rather than a re-partitioned, risk-ordered map.
